title: Family worship
hook: Reformed and Puritan homes read and prayed together daily

segments.voice: Yesterday, Puritan meditation: one truth, carried from the head to the heart. Your line was the saints' everlasting rest. Which line did you carry, and did it warm? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

A poem by Robert Burns follows a Scottish farm laborer home at the end of the week. Supper is over. The family pulls in around the fire. The father takes down the big family Bible, the one that was his own father's pride, and lays his cap aside. They sing a psalm. Then, Burns writes, "The priest-like father reads the sacred page." And he prays. A poet's picture, and a tender one. But in Reformed and Puritan homes, a scene like that wasn't meant for one Saturday night. It was meant for every day. Today: family worship.

Reformed Christians found the idea in the Bible. Moses tells Israel to keep God's words on their hearts, and "teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up." Home, road, bed, morning: faith spoken at the kitchen table, not only at the altar. Joshua says it in one line: "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD." And when Paul sends greetings to Priscilla and Aquila, he greets "the church that is in their house." A household could be a small church. Reformed and Puritan Christians took that at its word. The Church of Scotland set out a directory for worship at home: households were to pray together, read the scriptures, and sing praises, with the head of the house leading. The shape was simple. A psalm sung. A chapter read. A question or two for the children. A prayer. Notice what that does. It doesn't wait for Sunday, or for the minister. The father or mother who was arguing over the bills an hour ago now opens the book. The children who fidgeted through supper hear the same stories their grandparents heard. And the kitchen, for a few minutes, becomes a place of worship. Not every home looked like Burns's poem, and homes now look all kinds of ways: a single parent and a teenager, roommates, a couple, a grandmother and one grandchild. Some Christians keep the old pattern with a devotional book at breakfast. Some pray together at bedtime. The furniture changes. The idea stays: a household that stops, together, and turns toward God.
screen: `THE CHURCH THAT IS IN THEIR HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a psalm with someone at home. If someone is nearby, ask: can I read you something short? Psalm one twenty-one is a good one: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." Read it slowly, or take turns. If you're alone, read it aloud anyway, and keep in mind the people you share a roof or a table with, or once did. Then sit quietly for a moment, together if you can. If you pray, you can name each of them before God. The bell holds the time.
Family worship. A household stopping together at home to read scripture, sing and pray: the house as a small church.
Your line: the household at prayer. Today, at one meal or one bedtime, pause together before you begin, for one line or one breath of quiet. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: In some Reformed, Presbyterian and other Protestant homes, families keep daily family worship: reading a passage of scripture, singing a psalm or hymn, and praying together, often after a meal or before bed.

original.note: Hebrew: "my house" — the word in Joshua 24:15, "as for me and my house."

trapdoor: what you thought: family worship means going to church as a family.

what a scholar hears: Paul greets "the church that is in their house", and the Church of Scotland gave households a written directory for worship at home.

notes: Burns, 'The Cotter's Saturday Night': the big family Bible ('The big ha'-Bible, ance his father's pride'), the bonnet laid aside, the psalm, 'The priest-like father reads the sacred page', and the prayer are summarized from the poem; only the one line is quoted. Confirm the quotation.

The Church of Scotland's Directory for Family Worship (1647, date not stated) summarized: prayer, reading of scripture and singing of praise, with the head of the family leading. It also speaks of morning and evening worship; the voice says only 'every day', following the index hook. Confirm.
The simple shape (psalm, chapter, a question or two for the children, prayer) is a general description; confirm it is fair.
Romans 16:3–5 is Paul's greeting to Priscilla and Aquila; the quoted phrase is from 16:5 (also 1 Corinthians 16:19 'the church that is in their house').
Original: בֵּיתִי as in Joshua 24:15 (וּבֵיתִי, 'and my house'); check vocalization and pronunciation.
Practice is phrased so people living alone can do it.

Editor pass: the hook and fork reveal had Burns's order wrong (reading, then psalm); in the poem the family sings first ('They chant their artless notes'), then the father reads, then prays. Fixed. Hook screen 'NOT ONCE A YEAR' contradicted the voice ('one Saturday night'); now 'NOT JUST SATURDAY NIGHT'.
Audit (2026-10-02): 'The idea comes from the Bible itself' (narrator asserting a derivation) now 'Reformed Christians found the idea in the Bible.' Burns order (psalm, reading, prayer) confirmed.
